extracted.intended_audience: authors (especially early-career) and reviewers of manuscripts for ZDM Mathematics Education and similar mathematics education journals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluation criteria for preparing, submitting, reviewing, and revising invited manuscripts for ZDM Mathematics Education, including manuscript format, peer-review criteria, typical editorial decisions, and common author errors to avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript originality and overall contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: A manuscript submitted to ZDM Mathematics Education should be of high quality and make a significant contribution to the field. In addition, the article should be an original paper and not have been published elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers must follow the journal's author guidelines; invited papers still undergo rigorous peer review. Emphasises novelty and substantive contribution rather than anecdotal evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript length and language requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts should be no shorter than 40,000 characters including spaces and no longer than 60,000 characters including spaces, and covering abstract, references and a possible appendix. The papers have to be written in English (either American or British English).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors submit electronically via Editorial Manager; editorial office checks compliance with these formatting and language requirements. ZDM provides language editing support for non-native English speakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific quality: meaningful contribution and distinctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the paper a meaningful contribution to mathematics education research and is it distinct from other work of the author(s)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers evaluate whether the manuscript advances knowledge and is sufficiently distinct from the authors' prior publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific quality: originality of approach and insight
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the approach or the argumentation original and does the paper develop new insights into relevant research questions on mathematics education?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original argumentation and development of new insights are valued; avoid recycling known approaches without clear novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific quality: literature review adequacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the paper review previous studies and does it consider the relevant literature in the field? Does it avoid unnecessary self-references?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literature reviews must cover the current state-of-the-art and avoid being outdated or narrowly country-focused. For an international journal like ZDM, reviewers expect a broader, international view rather than literature limited to the authors' country or culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific quality: adequacy of theoretical framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the theoretical frame adequate, i.e., is there an appropriate alignment between the theoretical framework and the questions asked or the problems tackled?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong theoretical framework is indispensable. It may draw on established 'grand theories' but must carefully develop and define theoretical constructs and embed them in the study. Balance breadth and focus: the literature survey should be focused on the research question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific quality: methodological adequacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the methodological approach adequate, i.e., do the research methods and analyses match the problem or question?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodology must be embedded in an explicit research paradigm (qualitative, quantitative, mixed, design-based, interpretative, etc.). Authors must justify why chosen methods are adequate and necessary, describe sample and sampling procedure, and transparently report data evaluation processes (e.g., coding structure, code development, worked examples). Quantitative studies should report usual quality indicators; qualitative studies should include coding manuals or examples (appendix recommended) and careful translations of transcripts when applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific quality: consistency and justification of argumentation and claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the argumentations consistent, are the claims and conclusions justified in an acceptable way, do they follow logically from the data or other information presented?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should explicitly connect results to the theoretical framework and state-of-the-art; interpretations must be sufficient and logically grounded. Beware using an ambitious theoretical framework but producing only minor results without adequate interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation quality: title and abstract suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the title suitable and is the abstract distinct and adequate?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clear research question or research aim should already be mentioned in the abstract and function as an advance organiser for the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation quality: clarity and organisation of writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the writing lucid, clear, and well-organised?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers should have a clear structure; common first-submission problems include weak structure or unclear central argumentation. Editors expect lucid exposition to help reviewers and readers follow arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation quality: quality of figures and tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the quality of the figures and tables adequate?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figures and tables should be clear, well-labelled, and contribute meaningfully to the paper’s arguments and results presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer recommendation categories (decision options)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are asked to make one of the following recommendations: Accept without changes; Accept with minor changes; Accept with significant changes; Rewrite the paper; Reject the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guest editors and editor-in-chief base decisions on these reviewer recommendations; 'accept with significant changes' is common for invited papers and typically requires a substantive revision while retaining the paper's core.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewers' report expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are invited to evaluate the paper according to the journal's criteria and to write a commentary analysing the strengths, weaknesses and limitations of the paper and the research reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should make comments explicit, detailed and constructive to provide a sound basis for editorial decisions and to help authors revise. Reviewers may differentiate between comments intended for editors and those for authors. ZDM typically invites three reviewers (usually two for later rounds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision and resubmission requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors asked to revise must submit the revised manuscript and a letter to the reviewers and the editor-in-chief describing the changes made, in point form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This letter should explain what was changed and justify why any requested changes were not made (e.g., space restrictions). Revision time is usually two months; revised papers are re-reviewed (usually by the same reviewers). Two to three revision rounds are typical before acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended structure for empirical research papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Advisable structure for empirical research papers: Introduction (research question/aim as advance organiser); Literature review on the state-of-the-art; Development of detailed research questions/aims referring to the literature review; Description of the theoretical framework and important constructs; Description of the underlying methodology; Display of the results; Summary of results and interpretations; Discussion of limitations, conclusions, potential to generalise and further prospects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The recommended structure helps ensure clarity of argument and methodological transparency. The chapter notes this structure is particularly suited to empirical research; theoretical or constructive papers may adopt different structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential presence of a clear research question or aim
rubrics_metrics.description: A central error is that a clear research question or research aim is missing, leaving the central argumentation vague or unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors must formulate at least a rough research question at the beginning and in the abstract; details can follow after the literature review showing the research gap to be addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature review common pitfalls and expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Common problems in literature reviews include usage of outdated literature or non-consideration of the most recent literature, and reviews that are too narrow and country-focused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For an international journal, the literature review should reflect current, international scholarship and be directly connected to the research question rather than presenting a loose, overly general overview.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological reporting detail (coding, evaluation transparency)
rubrics_metrics.description: For qualitative and other empirical methods, the description of the data evaluation process must be detailed: coding structure, development of codes, worked examples, and parts of the coding manual (appendix) are advised. For quantitative studies, the usual quality indicators should be reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A short reference to a grand theory (e.g., Grounded Theory) is not sufficient; reviewers expect transparent, detailed descriptions so critical readers can follow and evaluate the evaluation process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of variability versus uniformity and generalisability
rubrics_metrics.description: Many qualitative studies aim to describe variability, whereas quantitative studies aim for uniformity; the variability of the data should be described and not restricted to extremely small-scale studies. Although most studies are not representative, authors should address potential to generalise or transfer findings to other contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussing transferability and limits of generalisation increases the relevance and scope of a study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Results interpretation and linkage to theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Results must be clearly described and interpreted with reference to the original theoretical framework and the state-of-the-art; avoid missing the connection between an ambitious theoretical framework and the results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide intensive interpretation, relate findings back to constructs/theory, and discuss implications and limitations; weak interpretation is a common reason for requests to revise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial office checks and language support
rubrics_metrics.description: The editorial office checks manuscripts for compliance with the guidelines and ZDM provides language editing for non-native speakers of English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should follow submission formatting and prepare for possible editorial language editing; support aims to help broaden international authorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical timelines and speed expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Based on reviewer recommendations a decision letter is sent by the editor-in-chief on average 60 days after submission. Revision time is usually two months. On average 16 days after acceptance the paper is available online at Springer Link with DOI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The process is described as fast and transparent; authors can expect usually two to three rounds of revision and relatively quick online availability after acceptance.
